title: The Alternative Beta Dictionary
about: A map of alternative beta: the systematic, rules-based return streams that sit between cheap market beta and expensive manager alpha. Each sphere is a concept; lines show how ideas lean on each other. Click a term to see its neighbourhood, or press / to search. Educational only, not investment advice.

terms.title: Alternative Beta
terms.summary: Returns from systematic, rules-based exposures to risk premia other than plain long-only market beta.
terms.body:
Alternative beta sits between cheap [[market-beta|market beta]] and expensive [[alpha]]. It packages well-documented return sources such as [[value]], [[momentum]] and [[carry]] into transparent rules that can be run at low cost.

The idea came from observing that much of what [[hedge-fund-replication|hedge funds]] earned could be explained by a handful of [[risk-premia]]. If those drivers can be captured mechanically, investors need not pay [[two-and-twenty]] for them.

Also called _liquid alternatives_, _style premia_ or [[alternative-risk-premia|ARP]].
usage: Is this fund alpha or just alternative beta?
Strip out value, momentum and carry and there's very little left. It's alt beta at a hedge fund fee.

terms.title: Market Beta
terms.summary: Sensitivity of an asset to the overall market; the return you get simply for holding the market portfolio.
terms.body:
In the [[capm|CAPM]], market beta is the only priced risk. It is cheap to own through index funds, so it is the baseline against which [[alternative-beta]] and [[alpha]] are measured.

Alternative beta strategies are usually built [[market-neutral]] precisely so their returns are not just disguised market beta.
usage: Our long-short book has a 0.4 beta.
Then 40% of that return is just the market. Hedge it before you call it a premium.

terms.title: Alpha
terms.summary: Return not explained by known systematic exposures; the manager-skill residual after accounting for betas.
terms.body:
Alpha is defined relative to a model. Under the [[capm|CAPM]] much of what looked like alpha later turned out to be [[value]] or [[momentum]] exposure once [[factor-model|multi-factor models]] were used.

This migration from alpha to [[alternative-beta]] is the core story of the field: yesterday's alpha is today's factor.
usage: Their Sharpe is great.
Run it through a factor regression first. Alpha shrinks fast.

terms.title: Risk Premia
terms.summary: Extra expected return earned as compensation for bearing a risk that others want to avoid.
terms.body:
A risk premium exists when investors demand payment for holding an exposure that hurts in bad times. [[carry]] strategies, for instance, tend to lose in crises, so they pay a premium in normal times.

Not every factor is a true risk premium: some are [[behavioral-anomaly|behavioral anomalies]]. The distinction matters for whether the return should persist.
usage: Why should carry keep working?
Because it crashes when everyone needs liquidity. That pain is what you're paid for.

terms.title: Behavioral Anomaly
terms.summary: A return pattern driven by systematic investor errors or constraints rather than compensation for risk.
terms.body:
[[momentum]] is the classic example: under-reaction to news and herding produce trends that are hard to explain as risk. Anomalies can be arbitraged away once widely known, which feeds [[factor-crowding]] and [[alpha-decay]].

Many factors are probably a blend of [[risk-premia|risk]] and behavior.
usage: Is low vol a risk premium?
More likely an anomaly. Leverage-constrained investors overpay for lottery stocks.

terms.title: CAPM
terms.summary: Capital Asset Pricing Model: expected return is linear in market beta alone.
terms.body: The CAPM predicts that only [[market-beta]] is rewarded. Empirical failures of the model, such as the [[value]] and [[size]] effects, motivated the [[factor-model|Fama-French]] family and ultimately [[factor-investing]].

terms.title: Factor Model
terms.summary: A regression that explains asset or portfolio returns as exposures to a set of common factors.
terms.body:
Fama-French three-factor (market, [[size]], [[value]]), Carhart four-factor (+[[momentum]]) and five-factor (+[[profitability]], investment) models are the standard toolkit.

Factor models are used both to build strategies and to measure [[alpha]] by stripping out known exposures in [[hedge-fund-replication]] and performance attribution.
usage: What's the R-squared on the four-factor regression?
0.78. Most of the fund is explained by momentum and value.

terms.title: Factor Investing
terms.summary: Deliberately targeting exposures to rewarded factors rather than to asset classes or managers.
terms.body:
Factor investing reframes allocation around drivers of return. A portfolio is described by how much [[value]], [[momentum]], [[quality]] or [[carry]] it holds.

Long-only versions are sold as [[smart-beta]]; long-short versions are [[alternative-risk-premia]].

terms.title: Value
terms.summary: Buying cheap assets and selling expensive ones, measured by price relative to fundamentals.
terms.body:
In equities value compares price to book, earnings or cash flow. Across assets it extends to currencies (PPP), bonds (real yield) and commodities (long-run price), making it a genuine [[cross-asset]] style.

Value suffered a long [[factor-drawdown|drawdown]] through 2020, reviving debate about whether it was a [[risk-premia|risk premium]] or a fading anomaly. It pairs well with [[momentum]] because the two are negatively correlated.
usage: Value is dead.
People said that in 1999 too. The spread between cheap and expensive was at record highs.

terms.title: Momentum
terms.summary: Buying recent winners and selling recent losers, typically over a 12-month lookback skipping the last month.
terms.body:
Cross-sectional momentum ranks assets against each other; [[trend-following]] is its time-series cousin. Momentum is among the most robust factors across markets and centuries.

Its weakness is [[crash-risk|momentum crashes]], sharp reversals after market bottoms. [[volatility-targeting|Vol scaling]] and combining with [[value]] soften the blow.
usage: Why skip the most recent month?
Short-term reversal. Last month's winners tend to give some back.

terms.title: Size
terms.summary: The historical tendency of small-cap stocks to outperform large caps.
terms.body: One of the original Fama-French factors. The pure size premium has been weak since its discovery and is sensitive to [[transaction-costs|trading costs]] and liquidity. It works better when controlled for [[quality]], i.e. avoiding small junk.

terms.title: Quality
terms.summary: Favoring firms with high profitability, stable earnings and strong balance sheets.
terms.body: Quality is a family: [[profitability]], earnings stability, low leverage and low accruals. It tends to be defensive, holding up in sell-offs, and complements [[value]] by filtering out value traps.
usage: Isn't quality just expensive stocks?
Often, which is why it pairs so well with value in a multi-factor book.

terms.title: Profitability
terms.summary: Gross or operating profits scaled by assets; a core quality metric and a Fama-French factor.
terms.body: Novy-Marx showed gross profitability predicts returns about as well as [[value]]. It is the P in the Fama-French five-factor [[factor-model]] and the backbone of most [[quality]] definitions.

terms.title: Low Volatility
terms.summary: Low-risk stocks have delivered similar or better returns than high-risk stocks, contradicting CAPM.
terms.body:
Also known as betting-against-beta. Explanations point to leverage constraints and lottery preferences, making it a [[behavioral-anomaly]] as much as a [[risk-premia|premium]].

Implemented long-short it must be levered on the long side to be [[market-neutral|beta-neutral]]. It carries [[interest-rate-sensitivity|rate sensitivity]] because low-vol stocks behave like bonds.

terms.title: Carry
terms.summary: Return an asset earns if prices stay unchanged: yield, roll-down or interest differential.
terms.body:
Carry generalizes the FX carry trade to bonds (yield + roll-down), commodities (futures roll yield) and equities (dividend yield). It is the prototypical [[cross-asset]] premium.

Carry is a true [[risk-premia|risk premium]] with nasty left-tail [[crash-risk]]: it collects small gains and loses big in liquidity crises.
usage: The yen carry trade just unwound.
Classic carry. Picking up nickels in front of a steamroller.

terms.title: FX Carry
terms.summary: Long high-yielding currencies, short low-yielding ones, exploiting the failure of uncovered interest parity.
terms.body: The oldest [[carry]] trade. Theory says high-rate currencies should depreciate to offset their yield; in practice they tend not to, on average. Returns are strongly [[skewness|negatively skewed]] and correlate with global risk appetite.

terms.title: Trend Following
terms.summary: Time-series momentum: go long assets in uptrends and short those in downtrends, across futures markets.
terms.body:
The engine of managed futures and [[cta|CTAs]]. Unlike cross-sectional [[momentum]] it can be net long or short everything.

Trend's prized property is [[crisis-alpha]]: it has historically done well in prolonged equity bear markets, giving positive [[skewness]].
usage: Why hold trend if it's flat for years?
For years like 2008 and 2022. It's the insurance that pays you to own it, sometimes.

terms.title: Term Premium
terms.summary: Extra yield investors demand for holding long-maturity bonds instead of rolling short ones.
terms.body: A bond [[risk-premia|risk premium]] tied to inflation and rate uncertainty. Bond [[carry]] strategies harvest it through yield and roll-down. It has been compressed or negative in some periods, and it drives [[interest-rate-sensitivity]] in many defensive strategies.

terms.title: Volatility Risk Premium
terms.summary: Implied volatility tends to exceed realized volatility, so selling options earns a premium on average.
terms.body:
Option buyers overpay for insurance. Short-vol strategies (selling puts, straddles or variance swaps) collect that gap but carry severe [[crash-risk]] and [[skewness|negative skew]], as February 2018's _Volmageddon_ showed.

Often sized with [[volatility-targeting]] and paired with [[trend-following]] to offset tails.
usage: The short-vol sleeve is up again.
It always is, right until the day it gives back two years.

terms.title: Merger Arbitrage
terms.summary: Buying acquisition targets after announcement to earn the spread to the deal price, bearing deal-break risk.
terms.body: Behaves like selling insurance on deals: steady small gains, occasional large losses when deals fail, especially in market stress. A standard building block in [[hedge-fund-replication]] and [[event-driven]] alternative beta.

terms.title: Event-Driven
terms.summary: Systematic strategies around corporate events: mergers, index rebalances, spin-offs and buybacks.
terms.body: Includes [[merger-arbitrage]] and index-inclusion effects. These premia arise from forced flows and deal risk rather than from classic factors, adding diversification to a [[multi-factor]] book.

terms.title: Defensive / Low-Risk
terms.summary: Cross-asset version of low volatility: overweight safer assets within each class, levered to target risk.
terms.body: Applies the [[low-volatility]] insight everywhere: short-duration bonds beat long on a risk-adjusted basis, low-beta equities beat high-beta. Requires [[leverage]] to be meaningful.

terms.title: Cross-Asset Styles
terms.summary: Applying the same factor logic (value, momentum, carry, defensive) across equities, bonds, FX and commodities.
terms.body:
The insight of Asness, Moskowitz and Pedersen: _value and momentum everywhere_. The same styles appear in every asset class, and the cross-asset versions diversify each other more than single-market factors do.

This is the core design of most [[alternative-risk-premia]] funds and [[multi-factor]] portfolios.

terms.title: Long-Short
terms.summary: Holding long positions in the top-ranked assets and shorts in the bottom-ranked, isolating the factor spread.
terms.body: The purest way to express a factor: the difference between winners and losers. Requires shorting, [[leverage]] and borrow, and costs more to run than [[smart-beta|long-only tilts]], but strips out [[market-beta]] to leave a [[market-neutral]] premium.

terms.title: Market Neutral
terms.summary: Constructed to have near-zero beta or dollar exposure to the overall market.
terms.body: Dollar-neutral means longs equal shorts; beta-neutral means their market sensitivities cancel. The two differ for factors like [[low-volatility]]. Neutrality lets [[alternative-beta]] be a true diversifier to equity [[market-beta]].

terms.title: Volatility Targeting
terms.summary: Scaling position sizes inversely to recent volatility so the strategy runs at a constant risk level.
terms.body:
Vol targeting equalizes risk across time and assets. It meaningfully reduces [[crash-risk|momentum crashes]] and is standard in [[trend-following]] and [[risk-parity]].

The trade-off is higher [[turnover]] and the risk of de-levering right before a rebound.

terms.title: Risk Parity
terms.summary: Allocating so each asset or factor contributes equally to total portfolio risk.
terms.body:
Instead of equal capital, risk parity equalizes risk contribution, which typically means [[leverage|levering]] low-risk bonds. It is itself treated as an [[alternative-beta]] and is the default weighting scheme for many [[multi-factor]] ARP portfolios.

Vulnerable to rising rates and stock-bond correlation turning positive, i.e. [[interest-rate-sensitivity]].

terms.title: Multi-Factor
terms.summary: Combining several low-correlated factors in one portfolio to smooth returns and reduce factor-specific drawdowns.
terms.body:
The main defence against any single [[factor-drawdown]]. [[value]] and [[momentum]] are negatively correlated, so blending them improves Sharpe dramatically.

Two designs: _mix_ (separate sleeves) or _integrate_ (a composite score per stock). Integrated approaches cut [[turnover]] and netting costs.
usage: Mix or integrate?
Integrate if costs matter. You don't want the value sleeve buying what momentum is selling.

terms.title: Leverage
terms.summary: Borrowing or using derivatives to scale exposure beyond invested capital.
terms.body: Most [[long-short]] premia have low raw volatility and need leverage to hit useful return targets. [[risk-parity]] and [[defensive]] strategies depend on it. Leverage magnifies [[crash-risk]] and funding-liquidity shocks.

terms.title: Turnover
terms.summary: How much of the portfolio is traded per period; the main driver of implementation cost.
terms.body: Fast signals like short-term [[momentum]] trade a lot; [[value]] trades slowly. High turnover multiplies [[transaction-costs]]. Rebalance buffers and signal smoothing reduce it at the cost of some signal decay.

terms.title: Transaction Costs
terms.summary: Commissions, spreads, market impact and borrow fees that separate paper returns from real ones.
terms.body: A strategy whose [[backtest]] ignores costs can look far better than it will trade. [[size]] and short-horizon factors are hit hardest. Costs also rise with [[factor-crowding]] as everyone trades the same names.

terms.title: Crash Risk
terms.summary: The chance of large, sudden losses, often clustered in market stress when diversification fails.
terms.body: [[carry]], [[volatility-premium|short vol]] and [[merger-arbitrage]] crash in liquidity crises; [[momentum]] crashes on sharp market rebounds. Crash risk is part of why [[risk-premia]] exist, and why [[trend-following]]'s [[crisis-alpha]] is valued.

terms.title: Skewness
terms.summary: Asymmetry of the return distribution; negative skew means rare big losses, positive means rare big gains.
terms.body: Sharpe ratio ignores skew, so negatively skewed premia like [[carry]] and [[volatility-premium|short vol]] look better than they are. Balancing them with positively skewed [[trend-following]] improves the whole portfolio's tail profile.

terms.title: Crisis Alpha
terms.summary: Positive returns during equity crises, the defining attraction of trend-following strategies.
terms.body: Coined for managed futures, which profited in 2008 and 2022. Not guaranteed: sudden V-shaped crashes can catch [[trend-following]] offside. Still the best-known diversifier to [[crash-risk]] in [[alternative-beta]] books.

terms.title: Factor Drawdown
terms.summary: An extended period of losses in a factor, sometimes lasting years, that tests investor patience.
terms.body:
[[value]] lost for over a decade to 2020; the 2018-2020 period hit most [[alternative-risk-premia]] funds at once. Long drawdowns are the main reason investors abandon factors, and a sign of possible [[factor-crowding]] or [[alpha-decay]].

[[multi-factor]] diversification is the standard mitigation.
usage: The ARP fund is down three years running.
Is the thesis broken or is this just a normal factor drawdown? Check the value spread.

terms.title: Factor Crowding
terms.summary: Too much capital chasing the same factor, compressing its premium and raising the risk of violent unwinds.
terms.body: The August 2007 quant quake was a crowding event: similar [[long-short]] books de-levered together. Crowding raises [[transaction-costs]], shrinks spreads and contributes to [[alpha-decay]], especially for [[behavioral-anomaly|anomalies]].

terms.title: Alpha Decay
terms.summary: The fall in a signal's returns after publication or wide adoption.
terms.body: McLean and Pontiff found anomaly returns drop roughly a third after publication. Some of that is [[factor-crowding]]; some reflects [[data-mining]] in the original research.

terms.title: Backtest
terms.summary: A simulation of how a strategy would have performed using historical data.
terms.body: Every [[alternative-beta]] product is sold on a backtest. Pitfalls include look-ahead bias, survivorship bias, ignoring [[transaction-costs]] and [[data-mining]]. Bank-sponsored [[alternative-risk-premia|ARP indices]] have shown large gaps between backtest and live results.
usage: The backtest Sharpe is 1.8.
Live Sharpe will be half that if you're lucky. What's the out-of-sample?

terms.title: Data Mining
terms.summary: Finding spurious patterns by testing many signals and reporting only the ones that worked.
terms.body: The _factor zoo_ contains hundreds of published factors; many are false positives. Harvey, Liu and Zhu argued new factors need t-stats above 3. Economic rationale ([[risk-premia|risk]] or [[behavioral-anomaly|behavior]]) and out-of-sample [[backtest]] evidence are the defences.

terms.title: Rate Sensitivity
terms.summary: Hidden exposure to interest rates in strategies that hold bond-like assets or rely on leverage.
terms.body: [[low-volatility]] and [[risk-parity]] both suffered as rates rose in 2022. [[term-premium]] harvesting is explicit rate risk. Good construction measures and hedges this unintended bet.

terms.title: Smart Beta
terms.summary: Long-only index funds that tilt toward factors or weight by something other than market cap.
terms.body: The retail-friendly face of [[factor-investing]]. Smart beta keeps full [[market-beta]] and adds factor tilts, so it is not a diversifier the way [[long-short]] [[alternative-risk-premia]] are. Usually delivered as [[etf|ETFs]].
usage: Is a value ETF alternative beta?
Only loosely. It's 95% market with a value tilt on top.

terms.title: Alternative Risk Premia
terms.summary: Long-short, multi-asset portfolios harvesting style premia; the institutional form of alternative beta.
terms.body:
ARP funds combine [[value]], [[momentum]], [[carry]], [[defensive]] and [[event-driven]] premia across the [[cross-asset]] universe, built [[market-neutral]] with [[risk-parity]] weights.

They are offered as mutual funds, UCITS or bank [[swap-index|swap indices]]. Performance after 2018 disappointed many allocators through a broad [[factor-drawdown]].

terms.title: Hedge Fund Replication
terms.summary: Reproducing hedge-fund index returns cheaply using liquid factor exposures.
terms.body:
Two approaches: _top-down_ regression of hedge-fund returns on liquid [[factor-model|factors]], or _bottom-up_ rebuilding strategies like [[merger-arbitrage]] and [[trend-following]] directly.

The premise is that much of hedge-fund return is [[alternative-beta]], not [[alpha]], and need not cost [[two-and-twenty]].
usage: Can we replicate the HFRI for 75bps?
Most of the systematic part, yes. You'll miss the idiosyncratic alpha, if there is any.

terms.title: CTA / Managed Futures
terms.summary: Funds trading futures systematically, mostly via trend following; named for Commodity Trading Advisors.
terms.body: The oldest systematic alternative-beta industry. CTAs are primarily [[trend-following]] with some [[carry]] and [[value]]. Their [[crisis-alpha]] made them popular diversifiers after 2008 and again in 2022. Widely available as [[liquid-alts]].

terms.title: Bank Risk Premia Index
terms.summary: A rules-based strategy index built by an investment bank and delivered to clients through a total return swap.
terms.body: Banks publish hundreds of [[alternative-risk-premia|ARP]] indices covering [[carry]], [[volatility-premium|short vol]], [[momentum]] and more. They are transparent and customizable, but [[backtest]] quality varies and embedded fees and [[transaction-costs]] can be opaque.

terms.title: Liquid Alternatives
terms.summary: Alternative strategies packaged in daily-liquid, regulated wrappers like mutual funds, UCITS or ETFs.
terms.body: Liquid alts brought [[alternative-beta]] to retail and smaller institutions: [[cta|managed futures]], [[alternative-risk-premia|ARP]] and [[hedge-fund-replication|replication]] funds. Liquidity rules limit [[leverage]] and illiquid holdings.

terms.title: Factor ETF
terms.summary: An exchange-traded fund tracking a factor index, the cheapest way to access smart beta.
terms.body: Factor ETFs made [[smart-beta]] mainstream at fees of 10-40bps. A growing set of [[liquid-alts]] ETFs now offer [[long-short]] and [[trend-following]] exposure too.

terms.title: Two and Twenty
terms.summary: The traditional hedge-fund fee: 2% of assets plus 20% of profits.
terms.body: The fee pressure that birthed [[alternative-beta]]. If returns are mostly factor exposure, paying 2/20 for them is expensive; [[hedge-fund-replication]] and [[liquid-alts]] deliver similar [[risk-premia]] for a fraction of the cost, leaving performance fees for true [[alpha]].
usage: What should we pay for this?
Beta fees for the beta, alpha fees for the alpha. Decompose it first.
